title: Trifid Nebula
caption: The central region of the Trifid Nebula (M20), imaged by Gemini North

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This image looks into the central region of the Trifid Nebula, also known as M20, in the constellation Sagittarius. Gemini North, the 8-meter telescope on Mauna Kea on Hawaii's Big Island, recorded it.

A favourite of photographers, the Trifid is an active cloud of gas and dust in which new stars are being born. Among the massive stars at its centre, one is thought to have formed approximately 100,000 years ago, which is very young by the standards of stars.

Star-forming clouds like this collapse under gravity into dense clumps that ignite as stars. Once massive stars switch on, their light and winds begin to shape and clear the surrounding gas. Despite how often it is photographed, the nebula's distance from the Solar System is still debated.
scale: The Trifid Nebula's distance is disputed but generally agreed to be somewhere between 2,200 and 9,000 light-years, according to Gemini Observatory.

understand.summary: The Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini North recorded this through g, r and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light. The source does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
understand.eye: The z filter reaches into near-infrared light beyond the eye's range, and an 8-meter telescope collects far more light than the eye.

explore: Estimates of the Trifid's distance range widely, because it can be difficult to measure how far away objects in our own galaxy are.
